newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan economy starting to strengthen--BOJ quoted.
newsitem.headline: Japan economy starting to strengthen--BOJ quoted.

text.p: Japan's economy is gradually recovering and is starting to strengthen, Bank of Japan (BOJ) Governor Yasuo Matsushita was quoted as saying on Friday.
Matsushita's comments, made at a meeting of economic ministers, were relayed to reporters by Economic Planning Agency Minister Taro Aso at a regular news conference.
Matsushita also said long-term interest rates were at around 2.3 percent and that short-term interest rates were generally below the official discount rate of 0.5 percent.

Aso also quoted him as saying that lending rates were moving at historical lows, while stock prices had recovered to around 18,000 on a key index in February. The yen had strengthened a bit to around 122 yen to the dollar while money supply growth remained at around three percent, Matsushita was quoted as saying.
Asked about the impact of the consumption tax increase to five percent from three percent in April, Aso said: "I don't think the impact will be as big as the general public thinks."
Although there would be some impact in the April-June quarter, the overall impact throughout the full fiscal year would not be such as to severely hinder the economy, he said.

Aso said the official estimate for economic growth for the current fiscal year was 2.5 percent, and external demand was expected to have contributed minus 0.6 percent. Meanwhile, the growth for next fiscal year, starting on April 1, was estimated at 1.9 percent with no contribution from external demand.
"The estimates reveal that we will achieve 1.9 percent growth only on domestic demand," he said.

Since most Japanese cars for sale in the United States were made locally, Aso said he did not think the impact of the weaker yen on exports would be as big as in past years. "I don't think exports will grow as sharply as previously on the weakness of the yen," he said.
Asked about the surge in Japan's current account surplus in January, Aso said: "If that trend continues, I am sure it could become a problem (with the United States)."

In order to avoid such a situation, Japan would take measures to help U.S. exports to Japan, Aso said. He added that a dispute with the U.S. over Japanese port practices could also become a major issue.
